title: A low-cost weekend in Myrtle Beach
summary: Beach days, free walks, state parks and a few well-chosen splurges
description: How to do a Myrtle Beach weekend on a modest budget: free beaches and boardwalks, state parks, low-cost mini golf and a plan for where to spend and where to save.
intro: Myrtle Beach has a reputation as an affordable beach destination, and it can be, but costs add up fast with a family. The good news is that the best thing here, the beach, is free. This plan keeps the spending to a few chosen items and fills the rest of the weekend with free or low-cost things. Prices change, so check each place's own page for current admission and rates.

sections.h: Where you stay matters more than what you do
p: Lodging is usually the biggest cost. Off-peak weekends in spring and fall are much cheaper than summer, and weekdays are cheaper than weekends. Rooms and rentals a few blocks from the oceanfront often cost much less than those directly on it, and the walk is short. Look for a place with a kitchen if you are traveling with a group, because breakfast and some dinners at home save a lot.

Arrive, drop your bags and walk the Myrtle Beach Boardwalk. It is free, it stretches more than a mile along the oceanfront and it is a good introduction to the area. Watch the sunset from the sand, and stop for something simple like ice cream or a snack. You do not need to ride anything or buy anything to enjoy the walk.

sections.h: Saturday: beach morning and a state park afternoon
p: Spend the morning on the beach. Bring your own chairs, umbrella and cooler if you can, because rentals on the oceanfront can be expensive. In the afternoon, take a short drive to Myrtle Beach State Park, which has a quieter beach, a pier, nature trails and a small entry fee. If you want a more remote feel, Huntington Beach State Park in Murrells Inlet has marsh boardwalks, a lagoon and a long beach, also for a modest fee.
Both parks are good places to bring a picnic. Check the state park system's own page for rates and for any seasonal changes to hours.

The Murrells Inlet MarshWalk is free to stroll, and it is a lively place to be at sunset, with live music at several of the venues. You do not need to eat a big dinner there. Walk the boardwalk, watch the boats and enjoy the atmosphere. If you do eat, look for early specials and shared plates.

sections.h: Sunday: a small town and a river
p: Drive inland to Conway or south to Georgetown for a change of scene. The Conway Riverwalk is a free waterfront walk in a pretty downtown with shops and cafes. In Georgetown, the Harborwalk follows the waterfront and is free to walk, with historic buildings a short distance away. Both are good for a slower morning before you head home.

list: One round of mini golf. It is a classic, and some courses are cheaper at certain times of day. Check each course's own page.
One special meal, rather than three. Pick something local, such as seafood in Murrells Inlet.
One paid experience, such as a dolphin cruise or an attraction your group will remember.
Disc golf, if you play. Splinter City Disc Golf Course is a county-run option, and it is a cheap way to spend a few hours outside.
Pack your own cooler for the beach: water, sandwiches and snacks.
Park a few blocks from the busiest areas to avoid premium lot rates, and check for free parking at beach access points.
Skip the souvenir shops until the end, and decide on one thing you really want.
Look for combination tickets or discounts on the attractions' own sites, rather than third-party sellers.
